title: Canada PNP Requirements 2026: Provincial Nominee Guide
metaDescription: Canada PNP 2026: how Provincial Nominee Programs work, the +600 CRS boost, streams with and without a job offer, and the step-by-step path to PR.
headline: Canada PNP Requirements 2026: Full Guide

sections.title: What is the Provincial Nominee Program?
sections.content:
Provincial Nominee Programs, or PNPs, let Canadian provinces and territories choose immigrants for the jobs and skills they need. The province picks the candidate and issues a nomination certificate, then Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, or IRCC, runs the security, medical and admissibility checks and makes the final decision on permanent residence.

Eleven jurisdictions run PNPs: Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, Nova Scotia, Ontario, Prince Edward Island, Saskatchewan, the Northwest Territories and Yukon. Quebec selects its own skilled workers through a separate system, and Nunavut has no PNP. Canada's 2026 Immigration Levels Plan targets around 91,500 to 110,000 PNP admissions, making it the second-largest permanent residence category.

sections.title: Enhanced versus base PNP streams
sections.content:
There are two pathways. Enhanced streams are linked to Express Entry: a nomination adds 600 points to your Comprehensive Ranking System score, virtually guaranteeing an invitation to apply in the next federal draw, and federal processing takes about six months after nomination. Base streams run outside Express Entry, need no Express Entry profile, and take longer at the federal stage, roughly 16 months.

Each province runs several streams targeting workers with job offers, local graduates, people in in-demand occupations or business owners. Some streams need a job offer, while others do not: Saskatchewan's Occupations In-Demand and Express Entry streams, for example, need no offer but require at least 60 points on the SINP grid and an eligible occupation.

sections.title: Eligibility requirements in 2026
sections.content:
Eligibility varies by stream, but most programs assess five areas: age, education, language, work experience and connection to the province. Candidates are typically aged 21 to 49, with points falling after 35 in most grids, and need at least a three-year bachelor's degree assessed through an Educational Credential Assessment from a body such as WES.

Language requirements are usually CLB 7, or IELTS 6.0 in all four bands, for skilled streams, although some entry-level streams accept CLB 4 or 5. Most streams want at least one to two years of continuous paid work experience in an in-demand NOC or TEER occupation, and test results must be less than two years old at submission.

sections.title: How to apply step by step
sections.content:
First, choose a province you would actually live in and read its official program pages, matching your occupation code, education, work experience and language scores to the right stream. Then create an Express Entry profile for enhanced streams, or submit an Expression of Interest to the province, and wait for an invitation or notification of interest.

Once selected, accept the nomination and submit your full application within the deadline, often 60 days, paying the provincial processing fee, which ranges from zero to about 1,500 dollars depending on the province. Then apply to IRCC for permanent residence. Total timelines run 9 to 24 months, and programs change often, so treat any guide as a map and verify the current rules on the province's official site.

faqs.q: How many CRS points does a PNP nomination add?
faqs.a: An Express Entry-linked provincial nomination adds 600 points to your Comprehensive Ranking System score, which virtually guarantees an invitation to apply in the next federal draw. Even a CRS score below 450 becomes competitive with the nomination. Base PNP streams do not use the CRS at all, because they run outside Express Entry and are processed on paper.

faqs.q: Do all PNP streams need a job offer?
faqs.a: No, not all PNP streams require a job offer. Saskatchewan's Occupations In-Demand and Express Entry streams nominate candidates based on skills and an Express Entry profile, with no offer needed, and some Alberta Express Entry pathways work the same way. Most streams in British Columbia, Ontario, Newfoundland and Labrador and Alberta's other streams do need a job offer or a local connection.

faqs.q: Which provinces have PNP programs in 2026?
faqs.a: Eleven jurisdictions run PNPs: Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, Nova Scotia, Ontario, Prince Edward Island, Saskatchewan, the Northwest Territories and Yukon. Quebec runs its own selection system and is not part of the federal PNP, while Nunavut has no PNP. Ontario closed its eight previous streams in June 2026 and now runs the Ontario Workforce Priority stream.

faqs.q: How long does the PNP process take?
faqs.a: Enhanced streams take roughly 8 to 10 months in total, with about six months of federal processing after nomination, while base streams run 18 to 25 months. Provincial stages vary: some provinces invite within weeks of an Expression of Interest, while others run draws on their own schedule. Always check the current processing times on the province's official site, because allocations and streams change during the year.
